canonicalExplanation.summary: C++ error messages can be long, especially with templates and overloads, but they have structure. Start with the **first error**, and within it the **line in your own code** (not deep inside `<algorithm>`). For **overload failures**, the compiler lists every **candidate** it tried and **why each was rejected** ("no known conversion from 'const char*' to 'int'"): compare your call's argument types with those reasons. For **template errors**, the "required from here" notes trace back to **your** call site: fix the types you passed there. Build with `-Wall -Wextra` and treat warnings as bugs.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner calls `add_item("pen", "3")` and gets 60 lines of errors mentioning std::basic_string and template frames. They start editing the standard headers' names in their own code at random. An overload failure is read from the rejected call outward, comparing candidate parameter constraints instead of editing every template frame. In this lesson you'll repair a set of syntax, type and link errors using compiler evidence.

```predict
{"question": "A 60-line error. Which part usually matters most?", "options": ["The longest line", "The first error at your own call site, plus each candidate's rejection reason"], "answer": 1, "why": "Long lines are usually just spelled-out type names."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Source-to-execution models**, **Editor and terminal workflow** and **Compile and link model** (preprocess, compile and link stages).

sections.heading: The model: call site, candidates, reasons
sections.body:
```cpp
#include <string>
void add_item(const std::string& name, int qty);
void add_item(const std::string& name, double price, int qty);

int main() {
    add_item("pen", "3");     // second argument is text, not a number.
}
```

```text
main.cpp:6:5: error: no matching function for call to 'add_item(const char [4], const char [2])'
main.cpp:2:6: note: candidate: 'void add_item(const std::string&, int)'
main.cpp:2:6: note:   no known conversion for argument 2 from 'const char [2]' to 'int'
main.cpp:3:6: note: candidate: 'void add_item(const std::string&, double, int)'
main.cpp:3:6: note:   candidate expects 3 arguments, 2 provided
```

| Read | Tells you |
|---|---|
| first `error:` line. | what failed, and where in your code. |
| each `candidate:`. | an overload the compiler considered. |
| the note under it. | exactly why it was rejected. |
| `required from here`. | the line in your code that triggered a template error. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why does the message say const char [2] instead of \"3\"?", "answer": "\"3\" is a string literal: an array of 2 chars (the '3' and '\\0'). The compiler reports types, not values, which is why reading types carefully matters."}
```

sections.heading: Warnings count

includes: Read the first error, the call site, each candidate and its rejection reason.
Follow template notes back to your own code and treat warnings as defects.

outcomes: Repair a set of syntax, type and link errors using compiler evidence.

examples.title: No matching function for call
examples.situation: An overload failure is read from the rejected call outward, comparing candidate parameter constraints instead of editing every template frame.
walkthrough: **Read from the rejected call outward:** main.cpp:6 is add_item("pen", "3").
**Comparing candidate parameter constraints:** candidate 1 needs an int second argument; candidate 2 needs 3 arguments.
**Instead of editing every template frame:** passing 3 instead of "3" will match candidate 1 and every note disappears.
examples.result: One small fix, guided by the evidence, resolves all 60 lines.

examples.title: The template error from sort
examples.situation: std::sort on a vector of Student structs produces errors inside <algorithm> about operator<.
walkthrough: The notes say "required from here", pointing at the sort call in main.cpp.
Student has no operator< and no comparator was passed.
Pass a comparator lambda, or define operator< for Student.
examples.result: The error is fixed at the call site, without touching library code.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The longest template diagnostic line is necessarily the root cause and all later notes describe separate defects.
misconceptions.correction: Long lines are often just expanded type names, and later notes usually explain the same single failure. Start at the first error in your code and read the rejection reasons.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, how many real mistakes were behind 60 lines?

analogy.example: Reading a C++ error is like **reading a delivery failure report**. The first line says which parcel failed (your call). Then it lists every address it tried (candidates) and why each failed ("wrong postcode"). You fix the label on your parcel, not the post office's route map (library templates).
limitations: Couriers try a few addresses; compilers may list dozens of candidates.
"Required from here" is the return-to-sender stamp.

steps.explanation: The overload failure is read from the rejected call outward.
The learner compares candidate parameter constraints with the call.
One change fixes it, instead of editing every template frame.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing an overload diagnosis. Step 1, Error: call is add_item(const char[4], const char[2]). The overload failure is read from the rejected call outward. Step 2, Compare: cand 1 is arg 2 must be int; cand 2 is needs 3 args. The learner compares candidate parameter constraints with the call. Step 3, Fix: call is add_item("pen", 3); errors is 0. One change fixes it, instead of editing every template frame.

nearTransfer.prompt: Fix these using only the compiler output: a missing semicolon, a call with the wrong argument type to an overloaded function, and a call to a declared but undefined function. Note the stage and the key line for each.

farTransfer.prompt: Trigger a template error by calling std::sort on a vector of a struct without operator<. Find the "required from here" line, then fix it two ways (operator< and a comparator lambda) and explain which is better for this type.
scaffold: Search the output for your file name.

remediation.explanation: Always: **first error, your file and line, the argument types, each candidate's reason.** Change your call to match a candidate, or change the candidate on purpose.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The template error from sort".

recap.summary: To repair errors using compiler evidence, start at the first error in your own code, compare your argument types with each candidate's rejection reason, follow template "required from here" notes back to your call site, classify the stage, and treat warnings as defects.
